issues.legal_issue: An eyewitness account is not rendered artificial or unreliable solely because it recounts the incident and the assailants’ individual acts with precision.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the eyewitnesses’ detailed accounts, including their descriptions of individual assailants’ acts, because the incident occurred at night.
The incident occurred on a moonlit night, and the trial court had heard the witnesses’ accounts and believed them.
The witnesses described the sequence and details of an exceptional violent incident, and their answers were elicited through questions in examination-in-chief.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony should not be rejected as artificial merely because it was precise; the trial and appellate courts were justified in accepting it.
issues.legal_principle: Witness testimony must be assessed pragmatically and from broad angles, not by rigid or exacting standards. An account may be detailed if the incident made a strong impression on the witness, and precision alone does not establish tutoring or artificiality. The court also considered the trial court’s opportunity to hear the witnesses and the possibility that the order of detail reflected the examiner’s questions. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused brought a criminal appeal challenging their conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_was_precise: An eyewitness gave a detailed account of the incident and the individual acts of the assailants.
predicates.trial_court_had_credited_account: The trial court heard the eyewitness account and accepted it.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction and the trial court accepted a precise eyewitness account, precision alone does not require treating that account as artificial.

issues.legal_issue: An injured eyewitness’s identification is not discredited merely because the witness had prior hostility toward the accused.
material_facts: One eyewitness sustained serious injuries during the occurrence and identified the appellants as assailants.
That eyewitness and the other eyewitnesses had reason for hostility because they had testified in an earlier murder case that resulted in the accused’s conviction.
The other two eyewitnesses supported the injured witness’s account, and the occurrence took place on a moonlit night.
issues.conclusion: The injured eyewitness’s identification was not likely to be a false implication based merely on prior hostility, and the hostility did not require rejection of the account.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the witness’s evidence in its circumstances, including the fact that the witness was injured in the same occurrence. It considered it most unlikely that such a witness would spare the actual assailants and falsely implicate the appellants merely because of prior ill feeling. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this assessment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused brought a criminal appeal challenging their conviction.

predicates.eyewitness_identified_accused: The eyewitness identified the accused as participants in the occurrence.

issues.definition: When an injured eyewitness with prior hostility identifies the accused in a criminal appeal against conviction, the hostility alone does not discredit the identification.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction in an earlier case does not necessarily extinguish a motive for revenge when the convicted persons remain released on bail pending their appeals.
material_facts: The appellants argued that there was no reason for them to seek revenge after the persons accused of killing their relative had been convicted.
Those persons had been released on bail while their appeals against conviction were pending.
issues.conclusion: The earlier convictions did not necessarily quench the appellants’ desire for revenge because the convicted persons remained on bail pending appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The court drew an inference about continuing motive from the circumstances: release on bail pending appeal meant the earlier conviction did not, by itself, establish that the desire for revenge had ended. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this inference.
